The Itanium architecture is obsolete
that any residual use of Itanium hardware in production is mostly HP-UX
or OpenVMS based. The use of Linux on Itanium appears to be limited to
enthusiasts that occasionally boot a fresh Linux kernel to see whether
things are still working as intended
column2: and perhaps to churn out some

column1: distro packages that are rarely used in practice.
None of the original companies behind Itanium still produce or support
any hardware or software for the architecture
'Orphaned' in the MAINTAINERS file
that contributed on behalf of those companies (nor anyone else
matter) have been willing to support or maintain the architecture
upstream or even be responsible for applying the odd fix. The Intel
firmware team removed all IA-64 support from the Tianocore/EDK2
reference implementation of EFI in 2018. (Itanium is the original
architecture for which EFI was developed
column2: and the way Linux supports it

column1: deviates significantly from other architectures.) Some distros
Debian and Gentoo
dropped support years ago.
While the argument is being made [1] that there is a 'for the common
good' angle to being able to build and run existing projects such as the
Grid Community Toolkit [2] on Itanium for interoperability testing
fact remains that none of those projects are known to be deployed on
Linux/ia64
column2: and very few people actually have access to such a system in

column1: the first place. Even if there were ways imaginable in which Linux/ia64
could be put to good use today
column2: what matters is whether anyone is

column1: actually doing that
column2: and this does not appear to be the case.

column1: There are no emulators widely available
column2: and so boot testing Itanium is

column1: generally infeasible for ordinary contributors. GCC still supports IA-64
but its compile farm [3] no longer has any IA-64 machines. GLIBC would
like to get rid of IA-64 [4] too because it would permit some overdue
code cleanups. In summary
column2: the benefits to the ecosystem of having IA-64

column1: be part of it are mostly theoretical
of keeping it supported is real.
So let's rip off the band aid
column2: and remove the IA-64 arch code entirely.

column1: This follows the timeline proposed by the Debian/ia64 maintainer [5]
which removes support in a controlled manner
good state in the most recent LTS release. Other projects will follow
once the kernel support is removed.
